name: Bayesian Linear Regression
analogy: Think of it as a straight-line fit that admits how much it does not know. Instead of drawing one line through the bars, it keeps a whole bundle of lines that are all plausible and tells you how far apart they would put the forecast.

steps.title: Start by doubting every feature
steps.description: Before seeing any data, the model assumes each feature's effect is probably small, centred on zero. This starting belief is called the prior, and it quietly guards against over-reading noise.
steps.inExample: All three features start with an effect likely to be small, somewhere between minus and plus a few points of forward move for every 100 points of feature.

steps.title: Show it the training bars
steps.description: The model looks at how each feature lined up with the outcome across the training window. Features that moved together with the outcome consistently earn bigger effects; noisy ones stay near zero.
steps.inExample: Across 600 bars, the 6-bar move shows a weak negative link to the next 6 bars, and volume shows almost none.

steps.title: Update the belief about each effect
steps.description: Prior and data are combined into a new belief that is a range of plausible effects, not a single number. With little or messy data the range stays wide; with plenty of clean data it tightens. This is an exact calculation, with no random sampling needed.
steps.inExample: The 6-bar move's effect is now believed to be near minus 3 points of forward move for every 100 points of recent move, with a range wide enough that zero is not ruled out.

steps.title: Forecast with all plausible effects at once
steps.description: For a new bar, the model does not use one line. It uses every plausible set of effects, weighted by how believable each is, so the forecast carries uncertainty about the effects.
steps.inExample: The new bar's features are fed through all plausible effect sets, which disagree by a small amount about the average move.

steps.title: Add the noise that no feature explains
steps.description: Even with the effects known exactly, future bars scatter around the forecast. The model adds this ordinary noise to the uncertainty about the effects to give the full predictive spread.
steps.inExample: The scatter of 6-bar moves around the fitted line is about 37 points, and the disagreement between plausible effects adds a little more, so the total predictive spread comes to about 38 points.

steps.title: Optionally tune the doubt by the evidence
steps.description: The strength of the starting doubt and the noise level can be chosen by asking which setting makes the observed data most believable, which avoids needing a separate validation split.
steps.inExample: The setting with the highest evidence keeps the starting doubt moderately strong, which suits a 600-bar window.

useFor.task: A forecast that states its own uncertainty
useFor.example: Predicting the MNQ move over the next 6 bars as an average plus a spread, so a trade can be skipped when the spread dwarfs the average.
Cutting position size when the predictive spread widens because the current features sit far from anything seen in the training window.

useFor.task: A steady fallback on short windows
useFor.example: Using it early in a walk-forward fold when a gradient boosting model would have too few bars to learn from.
Asking which of two feature subsets makes the training window more believable, without holding out bars.

avoidWhen: The link between features and outcome bends or has interactions, such as an effect that only appears when volatility is high; a tree-based or neural model captures that, and a straight line cannot.
You have very large amounts of data and many features, where the extra care about uncertainty adds little and speed matters.

example.scenario: On a 5-minute MNQ chart you fit the model on the last 600 bars to forecast the change in the close 6 bars (30 minutes) ahead, using three features. The newest bar has just closed.

input.summary: Three feature values for the newest bar, measured the same way as in the 600 training bars.

fields.name: move over the last 6 bars
fields.meaning: How far the close has fallen over the previous 30 minutes.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: distance from the 50-bar moving average
fields.meaning: How far the close sits below its recent average price.

fields.name: training window
fields.meaning: The number of 5-minute bars used to form the belief about each feature's effect.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The latest closing price, used to place the forecast in points.

output.summary: A forecast of the 6-bar move as an average and a spread, not a single number.

fields.name: expected move over 6 bars
fields.meaning: The average of the forecast; one point is worth 2 US dollars per contract, so about 4 US dollars.

fields.name: spread of the forecast
fields.meaning: One standard deviation of the predictive distribution, combining effect uncertainty and ordinary noise.

fields.name: 95 percent range
fields.meaning: The span within which the 6-bar move is expected to fall 95 times out of 100, if the model is right.

fields.name: share of spread from effect uncertainty
fields.meaning: How much of the spread comes from not knowing the effects exactly rather than from market noise.

example.reading: A plus 2 point lean inside a 38-point spread is a whisper, far below typical trading costs. The useful message is the width: this is a bar to leave alone, and the model says so honestly instead of handing back a confident-looking single number.
